## After this lecture you can

- turn raw text into model-ready units, and defend each preprocessing choice
- explain how byte-pair encoding (BPE) works, and work out how a new word is tokenized from given merge rules
- describe the distribution of word frequencies with Zipf's law, and the growth of the number of distinct words with Heaps' law
- derive a TF-IDF vector by hand and get the same numbers as `scikit-learn`
- explain, with examples, what a bag-of-words representation keeps and what it loses
- explain how differences between languages, such as Turkish agglutination, affect tokenization, vocabulary coverage and token counts

::: {.notes}
These are the chapter's learning objectives. In the book the fifth continues "and
justify in an interview which tasks the representation suits". We close the
lecture on interview questions.

The lecture follows the chapter's order. First units: how a text becomes tokens,
what each choice of unit gains and where it falls short, and how token counts
change on Turkish examples. Then Zipf's and Heaps' laws: how frequencies are
distributed, and how the number of distinct words grows with the data. Then the
core: six steps that take four short sentences all the way to vectors you can
measure distances on, with every intermediate number shown. Then what this
representation loses, which motivates the later chapters. And finally a real
experiment asking what these representations are good for today.

Every number in the chapter came from running the code shown, with scikit-learn
1.9, tiktoken 0.13, sentencepiece 0.2.2 and tokenizers 0.22.
:::

## The problem, in one sentence

::: {.lede}
The models in this chapter work on numerical input. Text is a string of characters.
:::

To give text to a model we have to turn it into a numerical representation. That takes two decisions:

1. [which units to split the text into]{.hl} — **tokenization**
2. [how to compute the value of each unit in the document vector]{.hl} — **weighting**

::: {.takeaway}
Preprocessing decisions are modelling decisions: every choice below is an assumption, and it belongs in your methods section.
:::

::: {.notes}
This chapter builds the bag-of-words and TF-IDF representations. They are the
sparse half of a field whose dense half we meet in Chapter 3 (Embeddings). Simple
models on sparse representations can be a strong baseline when labelled examples
are few, when long documents are classified by topic, or when exact word matching
matters. Such a model also helps to weigh what more complex methods gain against
what they cost.

Building these representations forces a series of *decisions*. Which units do you
split the text into? Which differences do you keep? Which units do you count?
Large language models involve similar decisions; there you inherit a good part of
them from the tokenizer that ships with the model. Here you make each one
yourself, so you can see it.

The sentence in the box is the chapter's margin note, and it is useful for the
whole lecture.
:::

## Split on whitespace — and watch it fail

```python
text = "The pump P-101 didn't fail; it's the seal (again!)."
print(text.split())
```

```text
['The', 'pump', 'P-101', "didn't", 'fail;', "it's", 'the', 'seal', '(again!).']
```

- `fail;` and `fail` are now different tokens. So are `The` and `the`, and `it's` and `it is`
- Each fix either merges things that should stay apart, or splits things that should stay together
- [The ways this fails are the entire design space of tokenization]{.hl}
- These are the problems of **splitting on whitespace alone**; a rule-based word tokenizer handles punctuation, apostrophes and URLs — what it cannot solve is new word forms that are not in the vocabulary

::: {.notes}
Before a model can count anything, something has to decide what a *thing* is.
That decision is yours, you make it once, and everything downstream inherits
it: how large the vocabulary grows, what counts as a word the model has never
seen, and — if a vendor bills you per token — what a sentence costs.

Nobody announces this decision; it arrives disguised as a one-line call to a
library. This section is about making it on purpose.

Vocabulary: *tokenization* is cutting a run of text into the pieces the model
will count; what counts as a piece is a design decision, not a fact about
language. A *token* is one of those pieces — often a word, sometimes part of a
word, sometimes punctuation. When a vendor charges "per token", this is the
thing being counted.
:::

## The normalization ladder {.smaller}

| Operation | [Possible benefit]{.pro} | [Possible loss or cost]{.con} | Recommendation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Lowercasing** | `Pump` = `pump`: two columns merge and their counts add up | `US` → `us`, `Apple` → `apple`; `str.lower()` does not apply the Turkish `I`–`ı`, `İ`–`i` mappings | Decide by language and task; with a pretrained model follow the model's own rules |
| **Removing punctuation** | `fail;` = `fail` | Can change identifiers such as `P-101`, decimals, URLs | Do not strip wholesale; choose which marks to keep by task |
| **Stop word removal** | Leaves the listed words out of the count: 43.9% of tokens here | If the list contains `not`, negation can be lost | Measure its effect in sparse count models; read the list |
| **Stemming** | `replaced` → `replac`: can gather forms under one output | Can merge different words (`university`, `universe` → `univers`) or leave forms of one word apart | Try it in lexical search and sparse models; look at the outputs |
| **Lemmatization** | `replaced` → `replace`: aims at the dictionary form | Can need a dictionary, rules or context; can err on ambiguous forms | Do not add it to a pretrained model; measure its benefit in sparse models |

::: {.takeaway}
The last column is a recommendation, not a rule. [Measure the effect on your own task.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
The example on the previous slide left three decisions: should `The` and `the`
count as the same, should the semicolon go, should `it's` and `it is` be merged?
All three are of one kind: erasing or keeping the difference between two
spellings. Normalization merges the spelling differences we want counted as the
same. Why not merge as many as possible? Because every operation also erases some
distinctions. The table puts each operation's possible benefit beside its
possible loss.

Lowercasing is mostly harmless for topic classification. In named entity
recognition (NER) capitalization is part of the signal, and lowercasing erases a
useful cue.

Stemming and lemmatization are both used to gather the forms of a word under one
form, but they are not the same operation. Stemming (Porter 1980) applies suffix
rules and does not guarantee that the result is a real word: `replaced` →
`replac`. Lemmatization aims at the form you would look up in a dictionary; in
English, telling whether `left` is the past tense of `leave` or a direction needs
context.

Look at what a stemmer actually merges: the Snowball Turkish stemmer used in the
book produces `kullanıyor` for `kullanıyorum` ("I am using") and `kulla` for
`kullandık` ("we used"), and does not merge the two.

"Which one should I use?" depends on the pipeline. With a pretrained transformer,
use the model's own tokenizer and the preprocessing it expects, and add neither.
In lexical search or a sparse classifier stemming can help. In Chapter 16's BM25
experiment Snowball raises the share of queries whose target document comes first
from 28.0% to 95.3%; that is the gain in that experimental design, and the same
gain should not be expected on real user queries.
:::

## Two steps that look harmless

### Lowercasing depends on the language

```python
"İSTANBUL".lower()              # 'i̇stanbul' — 'i' + U+0307, nine code points
"İSTANBUL".lower() == "istanbul"  # False
"IĞDIR".lower()                 # 'iğdir' — should be 'ığdır'
```

- Nothing errors. The result lands in a different vocabulary column from the `istanbul` a user types

### Stop word removal leaves nearly half the tokens out of the count

- `scikit-learn`'s English list has 318 words; on this corpus they are [about 0.4% of the vocabulary and 43.9% of all tokens]{.hl}. If the signal is in *not*, that information is left out too

::: {.notes}
This is the first mention of Unicode; introduce it in one sentence: the shared
table that gives every letter and sign of every writing system a number (`A`
is 65, `ç` is 231, `İ` is 304). The detail comes a few slides later.

Python's `str.lower()` implements the Unicode *default* case mapping — the
language-independent one. The standard defines language-specific tailorings
alongside it, and does not apply them unless you ask. Turkish needs a tailoring,
because it has two `i` letters and two `I` letters.

Chapter 4 (A Representation Bake-Off) hits this bug on a real corpus, and
Chapter 16 gives the locale-aware fix. The point here is only that
"lowercasing" is a language-dependent operation.

The stop word numbers are measured on the corpus used later in the chapter: 311
of the list's 318 words occur in it. A *stop word* is a word so common that some
pipelines throw it away before counting — *the*, *of*, *is*. Whether that is a
saving or a loss depends on the task. The 43.9% is a share of tokens; it does not
mean the text shrinks by that share in bytes, or the sparse matrix in memory.
:::

## One word at three unit sizes

Suppose `unbreakable` never appeared in the training text:

| Unit | How `unbreakable` looks | Result |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Word** | `<UNK>` | [Not in the vocabulary: the model gets nothing but the "unknown word" marker]{.con} |
| **Character** | `u` `n` `b` `r` `e` `a` `k` `a` `b` `l` `e` | [Nothing is lost, but one word became 11 units, and `u` on its own says nothing]{.con} |
| **Subword** | `un` `break` `able` | [3 units, each familiar from other words: `undo`, `breaking`, `readable`]{.pro} |

::: {.takeaway}
Who chose `un`, `break` and `able`? [Nobody did. They were found by counting.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.src}
Last row: how the `cl100k_base` tokenizer actually splits this word
:::

::: {.notes}
The problem of word-level tokenization is the fixed vocabulary: word forms not
seen in training are not in it. Character-level tokenization has the opposite
problem: sequences get long and a single unit carries very little. Subwords
strike a balance between the two.

This slide shows the three options on one word instead of describing them in
the abstract. The split in the last row is not made up; OpenAI's `cl100k_base`
tokenizer cuts `unbreakable` exactly there.

The question that leads to the next slide: who chose those pieces? The answer
is byte-pair encoding.
:::

## Byte-pair encoding: count, merge, repeat

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="35%"}
1. Start with characters
2. Count every adjacent pair
3. Merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol
4. Repeat

A four-word corpus: `low` ×5, `lower` ×2, `newest` ×6, `widest` ×3

[Nobody told it that English has suffixes.]{.hl} It counted.
:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
```text
merge  1: 'e' + 's' -> 'es'  (seen 9 times)
merge  2: 'es' + 't' -> 'est'  (seen 9 times)
merge  3: 'est' + '</w>' -> 'est</w>'  (seen 9 times)
merge  4: 'l' + 'o' -> 'lo'  (seen 7 times)
merge  5: 'lo' + 'w' -> 'low'  (seen 7 times)
merge  6: 'n' + 'e' -> 'ne'  (seen 6 times)
merge  7: 'ne' + 'w' -> 'new'  (seen 6 times)
merge  8: 'new' + 'est</w>' -> 'newest</w>'  (seen 6 times)
merge  9: 'low' + '</w>' -> 'low</w>'  (seen 5 times)
merge 10: 'w' + 'i' -> 'wi'  (seen 3 times)
```
:::

::::

::: {.src}
Sennrich et al. 2016
:::

::: {.notes}
Byte-pair encoding (BPE) is how the middle road of the previous slide is found:
it *learns* its units from data (Sennrich et al. 2016).

`</w>` marks the end of a word. Look at what happened without anyone supplying a
grammar. The first two merges build `est` — the English superlative suffix — and
the third attaches the word boundary to it, because superlatives are frequent.
It discovered `low` and `new` as stems.

The book shows the full merge loop in Python, and an interactive widget where
you type a word and watch the merges apply. Only 10 merges were learned
here, from a four-word corpus; a real tokenizer learns 50,000 or more.
:::

## A word it has never seen

```text
lowest   -> low est</w>
newer    -> new e r </w>
slow     -> s low</w>
widest   -> wi d est</w>
```

- To tokenize, replay the learned merges in the order they were learned
- `lowest` never appeared in training, and it is still cut into two pieces the model knows
- [As long as every character of a word is in the alphabet, an unseen *word* does not become `<UNK>`]{.hl}: in the worst case it is cut into shorter pieces
- Notice the condition: an unseen *character* still breaks this example. `çay` → `('ç', 'a', 'y', '</w>')`, none of them in the vocabulary

::: {.notes}
This is the main reason subwords won: in the worst case a word is cut into
shorter pieces. Representation quality drops; the input does not become
unrepresentable.

State the condition out loud: every *character* of the new word has to be in
the alphabet the merges were learned over. Ours came from `low`, `lower`,
`newest` and `widest` only. So `apply_merges("çay", merges)` returns characters
that are not in the vocabulary at all.

This is where real tokenizers differ from this small example. The next three
slides take it up: first the terms character, Unicode and byte; then starting
from bytes; then byte fallback.
:::

## Character, ASCII, Unicode, byte

- **ASCII** (1963): 128 numbers for the English letters, digits and punctuation. No `ç`, `ş` or `ğ`
- **Unicode**: one number for every character of every writing system — its **code point**
- **Byte**: a number from 0 to 255. **UTF-8** writes each code point as 1 to 4 bytes

| | `ç` | `a` | `y` |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Unicode code point | 231 (U+00E7) | 97 (U+0061) | 121 (U+0079) |
| In the ASCII table? | no | yes | yes |
| UTF-8 bytes | 195, 167 | 97 | 121 |

::: {.takeaway}
`çay` (tea): three letters to you, three numbers to Unicode, [four bytes on disk.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Students mix these four words up all the time, which is why they get a slide.

A character is a letter or sign as you see it on screen. A computer cannot
store letters, only numbers, so every character needs a number. ASCII is the
first widely used table that assigns them. Unicode is the same idea extended to
every writing system; the 128 ASCII characters keep their numbers in Unicode
(`a` is still 97).

A byte is the basic unit a computer stores data in: eight bits, 256 different
values. Unicode's numbers go far beyond 255, so a character does not always fit
in one byte. An encoding decides which bytes store a code point. UTF-8 writes 0
to 127, the ASCII characters, as a single byte and larger numbers as two, three
or four bytes.

You can show it in Python: `len("çay")` is 3, `len("çay".encode("utf-8"))` is 4.
:::

## Characters or bytes: what BPE starts from

::: {.lede}
A character alphabet **can be very large**: Unicode defines well over a hundred thousand characters. A byte alphabet **is complete with 256 values**.
:::

```text
çay   2 tokens  [b'\xc3\xa7', b'ay']
şişe  3 tokens  [b'\xc5\x9fi', b'\xc5\x9f', b'e']
ŞİŞE  6 tokens  [b'\xc5', b'\x9e', b'\xc4\xb0', b'\xc5', b'\x9e', b'E']
😀     2 tokens  [b'\xf0\x9f\x98', b'\x80']
```

- A tokenizer that starts from bytes has a complete alphabet from the first step: [no character is left unrepresentable; rare characters just take more tokens]{.hl}
- `ç` is one token: its two bytes were frequent enough to merge. `ŞİŞE` costs twice what `şişe` does
- The merges are not bound to character boundaries: `b'\xc5'` is *half a character*

::: {.src}
`cl100k_base` · Radford et al. 2019 · Gage 1994
:::

::: {.notes}
A tokenizer that starts from characters has an alphabet made of the characters
in its training text. However much text it sees, some character can still be
missing. A tokenizer that starts from bytes cannot meet a symbol it does not
know; every text in every language is a sequence of the 256 values.

The output is from OpenAI's byte-level `cl100k_base`. Read three things in it:
`ç` is a single token; capital `Ş` was rare in training, so its two bytes never
merged; the emoji is split the same way. A token can hold a whole character,
several characters, or only part of one.

A short note on history: the name BPE comes from a data-compression algorithm
published in 1994 (Gage 1994). GPT-2 introduced byte-level BPE with a
50,257-token vocabulary (Radford et al. 2019).

Keep two questions apart. A byte-level design guarantees *coverage*. How *many*
tokens a language costs is a separate question: it depends on how much of that
language the tokenizer's training data held. The measurement for Turkish comes
in a moment.

BPE is not the only way to learn a subword vocabulary. It has two relatives:
WordPiece, which BERT uses, and Unigram, which T5 uses. The book explains them
in Chapter 8, where it looks at BERT's tokenizer; Chapter 2 keeps a collapsed
deep-dive box for the curious. This lecture uses BPE alone.
:::

## Byte fallback: spelling an unknown character out in bytes

::: {.lede}
A third design: the vocabulary is built from characters, but one token for each of the 256 byte values is added to it.
:::

```text
byte_fallback=False  vocabulary  20  ['▁', 'ç', 'a', 'y']  ->  ' ⁇ ay'
byte_fallback=True   vocabulary 276  ['▁', '<0xC3>', '<0xA7>', 'a', 'y']  ->  'çay'
```

- SentencePiece was trained twice on eight Turkish words with no `ç` in them; both models were then given `çay`
- Off: `ç` gets the "unknown" id, and turned back into text [the letter is gone]{.con} (`⁇`)
- On: the two bytes of `ç` are written instead (C3 is 195, A7 is 167), and [`çay` comes back intact]{.pro}

::: {.src}
`sentencepiece` 0.2.2, `byte_fallback=True`
:::

::: {.notes}
The tokenizer handles the characters it knows as usual. When it meets one it
does not know, it writes that character's UTF-8 bytes one by one with the byte
tokens instead of writing `<UNK>`.

Tie the numbers to the previous slide: `<0xC3>` and `<0xA7>` are the two bytes
from the `çay` table (195 and 167). The vocabulary grew from 20 to 276: the 256
byte tokens were added.

The leading `▁` marks where a word starts; it comes back a few slides on.

The code for the experiment is in the chapter; fifteen lines.
:::

## Who pays for Turkish

::: {.lede}
Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, official English and Turkish texts, through OpenAI's tokenizers:
:::

::: {.roomy}
| Tokenizer | English | Turkish | Turkish/English token ratio |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| `cl100k_base` (GPT-3.5/4) | 170 code points → 33 tokens · 5.15 code points/token | 160 code points → 60 tokens · 2.67 code points/token | **1.82** |
| `o200k_base` | 170 code points → 33 tokens · 5.15 code points/token | 160 code points → 46 tokens · 3.48 code points/token | **1.39** |
:::

::: {.takeaway}
APIs bill per token and context windows are measured in tokens: [on this text Turkish takes more tokens for the same content.]{.hl} The ratio depends on the tokenizer and on the text; one paragraph does not give a general ratio.
:::

::: {.src}
Petrov et al. 2023
:::

::: {.notes}
Now the part that matters if you work in a language other than English. A
tokenizer is trained on a corpus, and how efficiently it encodes a language
depends on how much of that language the corpus contained — which, for the
tokenizers most people use, means mostly English.

Same content: the Turkish/English token ratio is 1.82 on the GPT-3.5/4 tokenizer
and 1.39 with `o200k_base`. Differences of this kind between languages are
documented and measured (Petrov et al. 2023). These two numbers, though, belong
to one short text; the last exercise repeats the measurement over many examples.
Lengths are counted in Unicode code points.

The measurement is a short `tiktoken` script in the chapter; students rerun it
on their own text in Exercise 1.
:::

## What a Turkish word costs

| Word | What the tokenizer sees | Tokens |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `ev` | `' ev'` | 1 |
| `evler` | `' ev'` `ler` | 2 |
| `evlerimiz` | `' ev'` `ler` `im` `iz` | 4 |
| `evlerimizden` | `' ev'` `ler` `im` `iz` `den` | **5** |

- *from our houses*: three English words, three tokens. [The same meaning in Turkish is one word and five tokens.]{.hl}
- The splits match the real morphology at three of four boundaries. The asterisk is `im|iz`: *-imiz* ("our") is a single morpheme

::: {.takeaway}
Bring Turkish text into one form before it reaches the tokenizer: `unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text)`
:::

::: {.notes}
Why does it happen? Turkish is agglutinative: meaning is built by stacking
suffixes onto a stem (Oflazer 1994). English builds meaning with separate words,
which is exactly what a frequency-based merge algorithm captures well.

The good news, with one honest asterisk. `ev|ler|im|iz|den` lines up with the
real morphology at three of its four boundaries — *ev* (house), *-ler*
(plural), *-den* (from) — and nobody supplied a rule of Turkish grammar. The
asterisk is `im|iz`: *-imiz* ("our") is a single morpheme that BPE cut in half,
because `im` and `iz` are each frequent on their own. Frequency is a good proxy
for morphology, not a substitute. The newer `o200k_base` cuts the same word as
`ev|ler|imiz|den`, so where the cut falls depends on the merge table, not on
the language.

One sentence is enough for the NFC line in the takeaway: a letter with a mark,
such as `ö`, can be stored in two different ways (one code point, or `o` plus a
separate "two dots" mark). The two look the same on screen, but a tokenizer
counts them differently. Every measurement in the chapter was taken after that
call.

Point at the space in front of `' ev'` in the table; it is the subject of the
next slide.
:::

## Where did the spaces go? {.smaller}

`evlerimizden geldik` ("we came from our houses") — the same two words in three tokenizer families (`␣` stands for a space):

| Family (tokenizer that was run) | Tokens | How it marks the word boundary |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **GPT** (`cl100k_base`) | `ev` `ler` `im` `iz` `den` `␣geld` `ik` | Glues the space onto the first token of the *next* word |
| **SentencePiece** (XLM-R) | `▁ev` `lerimiz` `den` `▁geldi` `k` | Puts a visible `▁` at the start of a word |
| **WordPiece** (multilingual BERT) | `ev` `##leri` `##mi` `##zde` `##n` `geldi` `##k` | Puts `##` in front of every piece that *continues* a word |

- **Pre-tokens first, then tokens.** The text is first cut at whitespace and punctuation into pre-tokens: **pre-tokenization**. [No token ever spans two pre-tokens]{.hl}
- To turn tokens back into text, where a word starts is written on the token itself
- SentencePiece does not pre-tokenize: it treats the space as an ordinary character and replaces it with `▁`

::: {.src}
Kudo & Richardson 2018
:::

::: {.notes}
Why does the `' ev'` token on the previous slide carry a space in front? This
slide is the answer.

GPT's BPE tokenizers and BERT's WordPiece do not apply their merges to the
sentence as a whole. They first cut the text into words (GPT-2 does it with a
regular expression) and only then split each word into subwords, inside its own
boundaries.

Cutting the text into words throws the spaces away. Ask the class: how would
you join the pieces `ev`, `ler`, `geld`, `ik` — as `evler geldik`, or as
`ev ler geld ik`? The only way to know is to write on the token where a word
starts. The three families do it with three different marks. All three show the
word boundary, but they do not carry exactly the same information in the same
way: one marks the space, one the start of a word, one the continuation of a
word.

That SentencePiece does not pre-tokenize is what makes it work for languages
such as Japanese and Chinese, which do not put spaces between words.

All three rows of the table were produced by running the tokenizers.
:::

## The four stages of a tokenizer {.smaller}

`Çay içtik, sonra evlerimizden çıktık.` ("We drank tea, then we left our houses.") — step by step through multilingual BERT's tokenizer:

| Stage | Output |
|:--|:--|
| **1. Normalization** | `cay ictik, sonra evlerimizden cıktık.` |
| **2. Pre-tokenization** | `cay` `ictik` `,` `sonra` `evlerimizden` `cıktık` `.` |
| **3. Subword encoding** | `cay` `ic` `##tik` `,` `sonra` `ev` `##leri` `##mi` `##zde` `##n` `cıktı` `##k` `.` |
| **4. Post-processing** (special tokens) | `[CLS]` `cay` `ic` `##tik` `,` `sonra` `ev` `##leri` `##mi` `##zde` `##n` `cıktı` `##k` `.` `[SEP]` |

- What the first stage deletes does not come back: the model [can no longer tell `çay` (tea) from `cay`]{.con}
- Subword encoding runs *inside* each word: `evlerimizden` is five pieces, `sonra` stays whole
- What reaches the model is not these pieces but their ids: `101, 21373, 11797, …, 119, 102`

::: {.src}
`bert-base-multilingual-uncased`, `tokenizers` 0.22
:::

::: {.notes}
Text goes through four stages, in order, before it reaches the model. This
slide follows them on one Turkish sentence; every row of the table is real
output.

Normalization: this tokenizer lowercases everything and strips the marks from
letters. `Çay` → `cay`, `içtik` → `ictik`. `ı` survived because Unicode defines
it as a letter of its own, not as an `i` with a mark added.

Pre-tokenization: the comma and the full stop became pieces of their own.

Post-processing: `[CLS]` is added at the start of the sequence and `[SEP]` at the end.

Tokenizers do not all fill these four stages the same way. The case-sensitive
version of the same model (`bert-base-multilingual-cased`) leaves the text
untouched in the first stage. GPT's byte-level tokenizers do no normalization
at all. SentencePiece skips pre-tokenization.
:::

## Special tokens

| token | function |
|:--|:--|
| `[UNK]` | input with no vocabulary entry; not needed for that reason when the alphabet covers every byte |
| `[PAD]` | padding that evens up short sequences in a batch; the attention mask ignores it |
| `[CLS]` | in the BERT family, the leading token; its representation is often used as a summary of the whole sequence |
| `[SEP]` | the boundary between two segments, a question and a passage for instance |
| BOS / EOS | start and end of sequence; in generative models EOS is how the model says it is finished |

::: {.takeaway}
The spellings differ by model — `<s>`, `</s>`, `<|endoftext|>` do these jobs. [Special tokens take their share of the context window too.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide closes a question students often ask: "what are those
square-bracket things in the tokenizer output?"

The `[CLS]` and `[SEP]` on the previous slide are what the fourth stage adds.
Count them when you count tokens; they take their share of the window.
:::

## Intuition check · characters {.question}

::: {.ask}
A character vocabulary is small, needs no merges to be learned, and in bytes never meets an unknown symbol. So why are subwords so widespread?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **Sequence length is the binding constraint**
- Attention grows with the *square* of sequence length, everything else in the layer linearly (Ch. 7)
- The same Turkish sentence: 160 code points → 25,600 pairs; 60 subwords → 3,600 pairs; 21 words → 441 pairs
- [Subwords strike a balance between vocabulary size and sequence length]{.hl} — BPE was a compression algorithm in 1994, but the goal here is choosing units
:::

::: {.notes}
Give students a minute before revealing (one click).

A character vocabulary is about 100 symbols for English, 256 if you work in
bytes. A full byte alphabet can represent every text; a hand-picked character
alphabet can fall short. The numbers in the third bullet are the chapter's
measurement: the Turkish text of Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human
Rights, under `cl100k_base`.

The tokenizer is the knob that trades vocabulary size against sequence length,
and BPE sets that knob using the statistics of the data rather than a human's
guess. The quadratic cost is Chapter 7's (Transformers and Attention).
:::

## Three granularities, side by side {.smaller}

| Criterion | Character or byte | Subword (BPE, WordPiece, Unigram) | Whole word |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Vocabulary size** | Depends on the chosen alphabet; a full byte alphabet is 256 values | Depends on the target set in training | Depends on the number of word forms chosen; the vocabulary in use is finite |
| **Out-of-vocabulary input** | [A character alphabet can fall short; a full byte alphabet represents every byte sequence]{.pro} | Alphabet coverage, the unknown-token rules and byte fallback, if present, decide | [Words not in the fixed vocabulary need an extra method]{.con} |
| **Sequence length** | [Usually longer]{.con} | Usually between the two | [A known word is one unit]{.pro} |
| **What the units correspond to** | Represents the spelling with small units | Pieces sometimes coincide with morphemes; not guaranteed | Keeps the word form |
| **Rich morphology** | Represents every form the alphabet covers | [Can reuse shared pieces across inflected forms]{.pro} | [The many inflected forms make vocabulary coverage hard]{.con} |
| **Tokenizer training** | A fixed alphabet needs no merges to be learned | Pieces are usually learned from a corpus | A word vocabulary is chosen or extracted from a corpus |

::: {.takeaway}
Unit size is a trade-off: [subwords strike a balance between vocabulary size and sequence length.]{.hl} Which design fits also depends on normalization, language coverage and fit with the model.
:::

::: {.notes}
Every tokenizer you meet sits somewhere on this axis. The two ends have opposite
limits: one struggles with vocabulary coverage, the other with sequence length.

The chapter makes the same comparison on a small example: a corpus of 60 forms
built from twelve Turkish stems in five forms each, and two words that are not in
it, `evlerden` ("from the houses") and `okullardan` ("from the schools"). The
whole-word vocabulary (60 entries) answers `<UNK>` for both; the character
tokenizer (18 symbols) spends 18 units; BPE stopped at the same 60 entries covers
them with six pieces: `ev ler den</w> okul lar dan</w>`.

The subword out-of-vocabulary cell has a condition: WordPiece, which cannot write
an unknown character as its bytes, can emit `[UNK]`.

WordPiece and Unigram in the column header are BPE's two relatives. The book
explains how the three differ in Chapter 8, where it looks at BERT's tokenizer;
Chapter 2 keeps a collapsed deep-dive box for the curious.
:::

:::

::: {.column .compact width="45%"}
- 20 Newsgroups training split: 11,314 documents; with `[a-z']+`, 2.29M tokens and 78,649 types
- Top 10 types → 20.99% of all tokens; top 1,000 → 71.04%; top 10,000 → 92.50%
- [About 49% of the types are seen exactly once]{.hl}; they are 1.69% of the tokens
- $f(r) \propto r^{-\alpha}$ — *approximately* a straight line on log-log axes. The dashed line is a reference, not a model estimated from the data
:::

::::

::: {.src}
Lang 1995 · Zipf 1949
:::

::: {.notes}
This section looks at two empirical relationships and keeps them apart from the
start. Zipf: how are frequencies distributed in a given corpus? Heaps: how does
the number of distinct words grow as the corpus does? Both are approximate,
observed regularities; neither dictates how tokenization has to be done.

A type here is each distinct string our splitting rule produces, and a token is
each occurrence of one. The numbers depend on the rule: the 11,314 documents are
the collection's training split, with headers, signatures and quotes removed and
the text lowercased.

The plot is a static copy of the book's interactive one: 50 ranks chosen at
logarithmic intervals. The line joining the dots is not a model fit. The dashed
line is the α = 1 reference scaled to the count at rank one. In the book you can
switch to linear axes: the differences between rare types get squeezed into the
bottom of the plot. The distribution does not change, only its appearance.

Single-occurrence types are *hapax legomena*: nearly half of the observed types
and about 1.7% of the tokens in this corpus. Whether all of them belong in a
model's vocabulary depends on the task and on how the vocabulary is built. Top
100 types → 46.99%.

"Approximately" matters. Taking the 106,425 occurrences at rank one as the scale
and choosing α = 1 predicts about 10,600 at rank ten; the observed count is
26,985, roughly two and a half times that. The Zipf–Mandelbrot form
f(r) ∝ (r + b)^(−α) gives the head of the distribution more flexibility; the
chapter does not estimate those parameters.
:::

## A regression slope is not a reliable Zipf exponent

::: {.lede}
Fitting a straight line by least squares to a log-log rank–frequency plot can describe the shape of a distribution. The slope alone is neither a reliable power-law estimate nor evidence of fit:
:::

1. The **range** chosen for the fit and the **weighting** of the points change the slope; the many rare types dominate an unweighted fit
2. Ranked frequencies are **not independent observations**; the uncertainty calculations of a simple regression can mislead
3. Estimating the coefficient, its standard error, and whether a power law is **an appropriate model at all** are three separate questions

::: {.takeaway}
The approach of Clauset and colleagues: maximum likelihood with a lower cutoff $x_{\min}$ estimated from the data; the fit is judged by comparing a Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance with synthetic samples — [not by an $R^2$.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.src}
Clauset et al. 2009
:::

::: {.notes}
Heteroscedasticity by itself does not make OLS coefficients biased; the third
point keeps those questions apart.

In the Clauset procedure the parameters are re-estimated on every synthetic
sample, and the power law is also compared with alternative distributions. The
exponent it estimates belongs to the distribution of occurrence counts; it is not
the same parameter as the rank–frequency exponent α.

The chapter does no such estimation, and no result in it depends on the exact
value. The notebook has a small demonstration of the argument.
:::

## Heaps' law: how the number of distinct types grows

- As the number of tokens processed, $N$, grows, the number of distinct types observed: $|V(N)| \approx K N^{\beta}$ — an approximate, empirical relationship
- On this corpus $K \approx 16.5$ and $\beta \approx 0.58$; the value reported for Reuters-RCV1 is $\beta \approx 0.49$
- The first 100,000 tokens bring 13,497 types; the last 100,000 measured bring only 1,814
- The fit is descriptive: the points are ever-longer prefixes of one token sequence, not independent samples

::: {.takeaway}
[New types keep arriving, but ever more rarely.]{.hl} That the model grows without bound is a property of the model; finite data does not prove it for a language.
:::

::: {.src}
Heaps 1978 · Manning et al. 2008
:::

::: {.notes}
With 0 < β < 1 the model grows while its rate of growth falls:
d|V|/dN = Kβ N^(β−1) > 0. The measured type count is a step-wise integer
sequence, and the power curve is an approximate summary of it. K and β depend on
the corpus, the document order and the preprocessing.

From these observations the chapter draws three practical points for vocabulary
design and feature selection:

1. A fixed word vocabulary may not cover new input completely: text whose topic
   and source are not restricted keeps bringing new names, part numbers and
   spellings. Subwords help represent those new forms with existing pieces.
2. Reliable statistics are hard to learn for rare types, yet a rare term can
   still matter. On this corpus, with the default `CountVectorizer`, `min_df=2`
   removes 62,208 of 101,631 columns (61%), and those carry only 3.4% of token
   occurrences. The stop word list removes 309 columns, which carry 43%.
3. How frequent a term is does not by itself determine how useful it is for a
   task. IDF takes spread across documents into account, and occurring in few
   documents is no guarantee of usefulness either. The next slide is the example.

The effect of `min_df` does not follow from Heaps' law; it follows from how types
are spread over documents.
:::

## Always look at your top-50 list

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="36%"}
::: {.stat}
[62,043]{.bignum}

occurrences of `'ax` — the **second** most frequent token, ahead of *to*, *a* and *of*
:::
:::

::: {.column width="64%"}
- Not a word of natural language: all of its occurrences sit in 13 of 11,314 documents
- Twelve of them are parts of a fourteen-part posting of a file called `roman.bmp`: file content encoded as text (uuencode)
- The largest single document contributes 11,147 of the 62,043; `'ax` is in only 0.1% of documents
- The apostrophe is in the raw data; `[a-z']+` keeps it in the token. Under the default `token_pattern`, `ax` is still second (62,387)
:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}
[Frequency in the corpus as a whole and spread across documents]{.hl} are different things. TF-IDF uses both, but a noise string found in few documents can also receive a high IDF.
:::

::: {.notes}
None of the thirteen documents is a reply: twelve are parts 3–14 of the same
file, and the thirteenth is a separate posting with another encoded file and a
single occurrence. Runs of identical bytes produce lines of the form
`>'AX>'AX>'AX`.

The apostrophe is already in the raw data; our regular expression keeps it inside
the token and lowercasing turns `AX` into `ax`. The content is the same; the form
of the token is a preprocessing decision.

The habit the chapter recommends: look at the list of most frequent tokens before
any weighting. It is a simple way to catch data and preprocessing problems.
:::

## From string to vector: six steps

::: {.lede}
Four maintenance logs — d1 `the pump failed` · d2 `the pump was replaced` · d3 `the valve failed` · d4 `the seal leak was repaired`
:::

| Step | For d1 = `the pump failed` | What it does |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Tokenize | `the` · `pump` · `failed` | text → units |
| **1** · Index | `failed`→0, `pump`→2, `the`→6 | every distinct term gets a column number |
| **2** · One-hot | `pump` = `[0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 0]` | a word as a vector |
| **3** · Sum = counts | `[1 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0]` | word order is gone |
| **4** · [TF-IDF weights]{.hl} | `[1.51 0 1.51 … 1.00 …]` | terms in few documents get a high IDF |
| **5** · [L2 normalize]{.hl} | `[0.64 0 0.64 … 0.42 …]` | the vector's L2 norm is now 1 |
| **6** · Compare | cos(d1, d3) = 0.528 | search, clustering and classification use these vectors |

::: {.notes}
The core of the chapter: four short maintenance logs taken all the way from
strings to vectors you can compute distances on, skipping no step and showing
every intermediate number.

This table is the chapter's pipeline figure. Every number is the one the code
actually produces for d1. The vocabulary index is alphabetical, so `failed` is
column 0, `pump` column 2 and `the` column 6.

The first three steps build the vocabulary and the term counts; the two
highlighted steps weight those counts by document frequencies and scale them by
the vector norm; the last step compares the vectors.
:::

## Steps 1–2 · an index, then a one-hot vector

```text
['failed' 'leak' 'pump' 'repaired' 'replaced' 'seal' 'the' 'valve' 'was']
```

- Nine terms: every vector from here on lives in $\mathbb{R}^9$. In real systems the vocabulary can reach tens or hundreds of thousands

```text
pump  : [0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 0]
valve : [0 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0]
        ------------------- multiply position by position
        [0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0]  -> sum = 0
```

- [The one-hot vectors of different words are orthogonal]{.hl}: `pump` is exactly as similar to `valve` as to `repaired`
- The vector encodes the word's identity, not closeness in meaning. Learned dense vectors come in Ch. 3

::: {.notes}
Step 1. After preprocessing and tokenization we sort the distinct terms and map
each one to a column number. That number is the term's *address* in the
vocabulary; by itself it says nothing about closeness in meaning. With its default
settings `CountVectorizer` lowercases the text and counts runs of two or more
letters or digits as tokens. `CountVectorizer().fit_transform(corpus)` followed by
`get_feature_names_out()` prints the output on the slide.

The order in which columns are numbered does not change any result, as long as
training and use keep the same mapping.

Step 2. The numerical difference between two column numbers says nothing about
how close two words are in meaning: `pump` at 2 is no closer to `repaired` at 3
than to `valve` at 7. The simplest encoding of a single word is a vector of zeros
with a single 1 at the word's address.

That vector encodes the word's identity. The dot product of *any* two distinct
one-hot vectors is zero; the vector of a word matches itself exactly (dot product
1). Closeness in meaning between different words is not part of this encoding.

One-hot is an intermediate structure here: a way to see how a document count
vector is built. To address the gap we move to learned dense vectors, embeddings,
in Chapter 3.
:::

## Step 3 · a document is the sum of its one-hots

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
- Add up the one-hot vectors of every token in a document: a **count vector**
- That is **bag-of-words** — the multiset of tokens, order discarded
- Do it for all four documents: [the document-term matrix]{.hl}, the central object of classical NLP
- A statistician's **design matrix**: documents are observations, each term's count is a feature
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```text
          d1  d2  d3  d4
failed     1   0   1   0
leak       0   0   0   1
pump       1   1   0   0
repaired   0   0   0   1
replaced   0   1   0   0
seal       0   0   0   1
the        1   1   1   1
valve      0   0   1   0
was        0   1   0   1
```
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
One word, one vector. But we set out to compare *documents*, and a document is
many words at once. The simplest possible answer works: add them up.

`d1 tokens: ['the', 'pump', 'failed']` → `d1 vector: [1 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0]`.

The matrix is shown transposed so it fits — it is 4 documents × 9 terms; rows
are documents, columns are words.

A *feature* is a variable that describes an observation. Here each feature says
how many times a particular term occurs in the document, and it is one column of
the matrix. For statisticians it is a predictor variable under a different name:
a design matrix with many correlated, mostly-zero predictors. Regularization,
feature selection and generalization need attention here as well.
:::

## Step 4 · does every word deserve the same weight?

::: {.lede}
`the` is in all four documents and distinguishes nothing; `valve` alone makes d3 distinctive. Raw counts treat them the same.
:::

$$\mathrm{idf}(t) = \ln\!\left(\frac{1 + n}{1 + \mathrm{df}(t)}\right) + 1$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column .compact width="47%"}
- $n = 4$. `pump` is in 2 documents: $\ln\frac{5}{3} + 1 = 1.511$
- `the` is in all 4: $\ln\frac{5}{5} + 1 = 1$ — [not zeroed out; it gets the smallest IDF factor]{.hl}
- The $1+$ terms act as one extra document containing every term once
:::

::: {.column width="53%"}
| On 20 Newsgroups | df | df/N | idf |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| `the` | 9,477 | 0.838 | 1.18 |
| `is` | 7,034 | 0.622 | 1.48 |
| `car` | 394 | 0.035 | 4.35 |
| `encryption` | 169 | 0.015 | 5.20 |
| `gravitational` | 8 | 0.001 | 8.14 |
:::

::::

::: {.src}
Spärck Jones 1972
:::

::: {.notes}
We have term counts. Now we decide how much weight each term should get when we
compare documents: high when the term is frequent *in this document* and found
*in few documents*. Splitting that into two factors gives TF-IDF.

Term frequency is the *raw* count; scikit-learn does not divide it by document
length. Had we divided by length first, the same IDF and the L2 normalization in
step 5 would still give the same vector: a common positive factor applied to
every component of a row cancels in the final division. Many textbooks define
tf = c(t,d)/|d| or 1 + log c(t,d). In SMART notation — tf × idf × normalization —
scikit-learn's default is summarized roughly as `ntc`; that code does not specify
the details of IDF smoothing, so the full formula has to be written out.
`sublinear_tf=True` switches the TF component to the logarithmic weight.

Document frequency (df) is how many documents contain the word at all. We want the
weight to fall as df rises, so we invert it. Raw inversion makes the range far too
wide, hence the logarithm (Spärck Jones 1972).

Reading the formula: the imaginary extra document explains why the denominator
1 + df always stays positive. For a fixed n the IDF is finite; as n grows, that
upper bound grows too. The add-one here resembles the Laplace smoothing of
Chapter 6; the denominators of the two formulas are not the same. The trailing +1
makes the IDF of a term that occurs in every document 1 rather than 0. This is
scikit-learn's exact formula; other libraries differ in the details.

The arithmetic: ln(1.667) + 1 = 0.511 + 1 = 1.511. For `the` the ratio falls to
1, the log to 0, and the term is left on the floor IDF value of 1: `pump` gets a
factor of 1.51 and `the` a factor of 1. On the small corpus every word unique to
one document gets 1.9163, and the largest absolute difference between the hand
computation and `idf_` is 0.0.

The librarian's version: ask for "the book about pumps". *the* narrows the shelf
down not at all; *pumps* narrows it to a metre of shelving. IDF weights a term
inversely to how widespread it is across documents.

The book's interactive IDF curve: the same increase in the share of documents
changes the weight more at low shares, and at higher shares the IDF still keeps
falling. The curve shows how widespread a term is, not whether it is a content
word.
:::

## Intuition check · the logarithm {.question}

::: {.ask}
Why does IDF use a logarithm?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **It compresses the range** — in 10,000 documents $1/\mathrm{df}$ gives a term found in one document ten thousand times the weight of a term found in all; $\log(n/\mathrm{df})$ stays between 9.2 and 0 and treats equal ratios equally
- **Its relation to self-information** — if a document is drawn with equal probability, $P(t) = \mathrm{df}(t)/n$ and $\log \frac{n}{\mathrm{df}(t)} = -\log P(t)$: the *self-information* of the event "this document contains $t$"
- That reading does not guarantee that the term matters semantically or is useful for every task
- Spärck Jones proposed IDF on empirical grounds in 1972; [the theoretical readings were developed later]{.hl}
:::

::: {.src}
Spärck Jones 1972 · Robertson 2004
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask the room before revealing (one click).

Range: $1/\mathrm{df}$ is also a decreasing, flattening curve; the difference is
the range of the weights. A ten-thousandfold ratio can inflate the effect of rare
shared terms in some comparisons. With the log, raising df from 1 to 10 costs the
same weight (ln 10 ≈ 2.3) as raising it from 1,000 to 10,000.

Self-information: this reading rests on a particular probability model, in which
documents are drawn with equal probability and the event is that the drawn
document contains the term. Robertson (2004) is the careful treatment.

Its relation to Zipf: a logarithm turns ratios into differences, which is why log
transforms are common for skewed quantities such as income or city size. But the
total frequency of use in Zipf's law and the document frequency in IDF are
different quantities.
:::

## Step 5 · multiply, then normalize

```text
counts        : [1 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0]
times idf     : [1.5108 0. 1.5108 0. 0. 0. 1. 0. 0.]
l2 norm       : 2.3591
normalized    : [0.6404 0. 0.6404 0. 0. 0. 0.4239 0. 0.]
sklearn row d1: [0.6404 0. 0.6404 0. 0. 0. 0.4239 0. 0.]
```

$$\lVert v \rVert_2 = \sqrt{1.5108^2 + 1.5108^2 + 1.0000^2} \approx 2.3591 \qquad \tfrac{1.5108}{2.3591} = 0.6404 \qquad \tfrac{1.0000}{2.3591} = 0.4239$$

- The hand computation and `TfidfVectorizer` agree to the four decimals shown; on this example the unrounded difference is 0.0 as well
- [L2 normalization changes how a model uses the size of the vector]{.hl}: without it, dot-product and Euclidean comparisons become partly comparisons of size
- On the unit sphere only *direction*, the weighted mix of terms, is left in the comparison

::: {.notes}
TF-IDF is the product, computed cell by cell. d1 has three non-zero positions,
each with a count of 1: 1.5108 for `failed`, 1.5108 for `pump`, 1.0000 for `the`.
The length is the ordinary Pythagorean one extended to nine dimensions — square,
add, take the root: √(2.28259 + 2.28259 + 1.00000) = √5.56518 ≈ 2.3591.
Intermediate values are rounded for display; at full precision the norm is
2.35906509…, which is what the library uses.

The six zero entries do not change the sum. To benefit from that on large
vocabularies the matrix is kept sparse; the `toarray()` here is only for
displaying intermediate values.

In longer documents some counts and the vector norm can grow, but not every
term's count necessarily does. L2 normalization brings the norm of a non-zero
vector to 1 while keeping the ratios between its components. It is useful when we
want the size effect removed; its effect on classification accuracy is measured
on validation data.

A document left with no active term after preprocessing gives the zero vector:
empty text, only out-of-vocabulary terms, or every term filtered out. Its norm is
0 and cosine with it is 0/0, undefined. scikit-learn returns a zero row and a
cosine of 0, a convention. Count these rows and handle them separately; do not
read the 0 as a measured dissimilarity between two valid documents.

This combination is not the only one anyone tried: Salton & Buckley (1988)
compared different weighting schemes empirically. Raw TF, smoothed IDF and L2 is
scikit-learn's default; other tools may choose a different formula.

The book's interactive matrix: in d3's row `the` and `valve` get the same raw
count, 1; under TF-IDF `the` is the smallest non-zero weight in each row, while
`valve`, found only in d3, is one of the darkest cells in the matrix.
:::

## Step 6 · cosine similarity

$$\cos(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert} = \sum_{i} a_i b_i \quad \text{(when both are unit length)}$$

$$\cos(\text{d1}, \text{d3}) = \underbrace{0.6404 \times 0.5729}_{\texttt{failed}} + \underbrace{0.4239 \times 0.3792}_{\texttt{the}} = 0.3669 + 0.1607 = 0.528$$

- `failed` supplies 70% of the similarity and `the` 30% — though each occurs exactly once in each document
- [The weighting is what decides which shared word counts as evidence]{.hl}
- d1 and d4 share only `the`: cosine 0.26 under raw counts, 0.11 under TF-IDF
- A cosine is the cosine of an angle — not a calibrated "26% similar"

::: {.notes}
Every document is now a point in R⁹. The question we can ask is: how similar are
the weighted term mixes of these two documents? For the non-zero vectors without
negative components used here, 1 means identical direction and 0 means no shared
term with positive weight. The score alone does not prove that two documents
share a topic or a meaning.

Only positions where *both* vectors are non-zero can contribute, so the
nine-dimensional sum has exactly two live terms. Under raw counts the two shared
words would have contributed equally.

Full matrices from the chapter, TF-IDF then raw counts:

- d1–d2 0.458 (raw 0.577); d1–d3 0.528 (0.667); d1–d4 0.112 (0.258)
- d2–d3 0.125 (0.289); d2–d4 0.286 (0.447); d3–d4 0.100 (0.258)

Every score between different documents drops, and the proportional drop is
largest for the pairs that share only `the`. Each document's similarity with
itself stays at 1.
:::

## Why cosine and not Euclidean distance?

::: {.takeaway}
On unit vectors $\lVert a - b \rVert^2 = 2 - 2\cos(a,b)$: here $2 - 2(0.651) = 0.698$, a distance of 0.836. [If non-zero vectors were normalized first, Euclid and cosine rank every pair the same.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Because on unnormalized vectors Euclidean distance is strongly affected by vector
magnitude. Two reports of the same failure can produce vectors of different
*magnitude* but similar *direction* if their term proportions are similar; the
extra detail in a longer report can change the direction too. Cosine looks only
at direction: it compares the proportions of the terms, not their total amount.

The figure: both axes use the same scale. Every count of B is exactly ten times
A's, so the two lie on one ray; C has different term proportions. On raw counts,
Euclidean distance puts A more than six times closer to C than to B. After L2
normalization A and B become the same point, and the only thing left to measure
is the angle.

Where 2 − 2cos comes from, worth doing once:
‖a − b‖² = (a − b)·(a − b) = a·a − 2(a·b) + b·b. On unit vectors a·a = b·b = 1
and a·b is the cosine, so ‖a − b‖² = 1 − 2cos + 1 = 2 − 2cos.

Distance is a strictly decreasing function of similarity. If non-zero vectors
have been L2-normalized, the two measures give the same ranking in an exact
nearest-neighbour search. Thresholds have to be converted, and the equivalence
does not mean every clustering method or approximate search implementation
returns the same result. Without normalization the equivalence no longer holds:
L2 distance is affected by both magnitude and direction, and documents with a
similar mix of terms can look far apart. The identity turns up again in Chapter 3
whenever someone swaps a cosine index for an L2 index.
:::

## What bag-of-words cannot do

| Not encoded directly | Two documents | Under bag-of-words |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Word order** | *the pump failed and the valve is fine* / *the valve failed and the pump is fine* | the same point: identical vectors, cosine 1.0 |
| **Scope of negation** | *no leak was found* / *a leak was found* | cosine 0.866 (counts), 0.777 (TF-IDF) — identical vectors if *no* is a stop word |
| **Synonymy** | *pump failed* / *pump broke* | share nothing beyond `pump` |
| **Polysemy** | `Apple` the company / `apple` the fruit | the same column |

::: {.takeaway}
Bigrams recover part of the order information (cosine 0.714 on the first pair). In the chapter's experiment they took the features from 32,318 to 249,522 [and accuracy fell.]{.hl} For long-range relations, Ch. 7.
:::

::: {.notes}
These losses explain why the order- and context-based representations of the
later chapters are needed.

Word order: not represented at all. Two reports naming opposite pieces of failed
equipment are the same point in space; the vectors are identical, so no
classifier can separate them. With bigrams the vocabulary grows and the pair
becomes distinguishable. That gain has a cost: on real corpora an n-gram
vocabulary can become very large (7.7× in the chapter's experiment); how large
depends on the corpus, the n-gram range and the filters.

Negation: *no* is a feature like any other; if it is kept, the two vectors differ
and a classifier can use the difference. What single-word counts do not encode
directly is *which expression* the negation attaches to. The example shows that
sentences with opposite meanings can get a high cosine. scikit-learn's built-in
English stop word list contains *no*; with it the two vectors become identical.
In tasks where negation changes the decision, check the stop word list
separately.

Synonymy and polysemy: different terms sit in separate columns, and the semantic
relation between them is not encoded directly. The dense representations of
Chapter 3 help to learn those relations; separating the senses a word takes in
different uses additionally needs context.
:::

## Does any of this still matter?

::: {.lede}
A real experiment: four newsgroups, 2,327 training and 1,550 test documents, logistic regression; no hyperparameter search.
:::

::: {.roomy}
| Setup | Accuracy | Features |
|:--|--:|--:|
| raw counts | 0.767 | 32,318 |
| counts + stop words | 0.795 | 32,014 |
| tf-idf | 0.831 | 32,318 |
| tf-idf + stop words | **0.853** | 32,014 |
| tf-idf + bigrams | 0.819 | 249,522 |
| tf-idf + sublinear tf | 0.843 | 32,318 |
:::

::: {.notes}
Yes — and students should be able to say why with numbers rather than opinion.

The categories are sci.med, sci.space, rec.autos and talk.politics.guns, with
headers, footers and quotes removed. Each setup is a scikit-learn pipeline of a
vectorizer and `LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)`. The results are
deterministic: the default lbfgs solver takes no randomness. The full code is
in the chapter; Exercise 4 reproduces it.

Ask the room to read the six lines before the next slide: what would you
conclude?
:::

## Four conclusions — and their uncertainty

1. **TF-IDF is worth 6.4 accuracy points** over raw counts — without more data or a hyperparameter search
2. **Stop word removal helps here** (+2.2) — on topic classification; it can hurt if the list removes words that matter for the task
3. **Accuracy fell when bigrams were added**, while the features grew 7.7-fold: more features do not guarantee higher accuracy
4. **`sublinear_tf` is slightly better** (0.843 vs 0.831): $1 + \log(\text{tf})$ in place of the raw count

::: {.takeaway}
The six models were measured on the same test documents, so differences call for a paired test. McNemar, with the threshold corrected for four comparisons at 0.0125: [differences 1, 2 and 4 fall below it; the bigram difference (p = 0.018) does not.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
These are point estimates with no intervals attached. Under a binomial
approximation that treats documents as independent, a single accuracy near 0.83
on 1,550 documents carries a 95% interval of roughly ±1.9 points; if two
accuracies were independent, their difference would carry roughly ±2.6. But the
six models see the same test documents, so the uncertainty of a difference has to
come from the paired predictions.

McNemar's test (McNemar 1947) compares the number of documents one model
classifies correctly and the other incorrectly. The chapter's measurement (only
the first correct / only the second correct / exact p-value):

- TF-IDF and raw counts: 119 / 20 / 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁸
- TF-IDF + stop words and TF-IDF: 86 / 52 / 0.0048
- TF-IDF + bigrams and TF-IDF: 17 / 35 / 0.018
- TF-IDF + sublinear tf and TF-IDF: 29 / 11 / 0.0064

These p-values measure only the uncertainty from sampling the test documents:
one train–test split, one training run.

On the stop word list: scikit-learn's own documentation calls
`stop_words='english'` problematic. It is not a general-purpose list, its
selection criteria are undocumented, and a few entries can never be produced by
the default `token_pattern`. If stop words matter to your result, write the list
yourself and print it.

On generalising: every number comes from English topic classification on long
documents, and two of the four conclusions can reverse when the task changes. On
Turkish product reviews — short documents, sentiment rather than topic — Chapter
4 measures the opposite on both: bigrams give the largest gain and plain counting
beats TF-IDF. That chapter's ablation shows the second result does not come from
IDF but from L2 normalization interacting with an untuned `C`, and that it
reverses under an equal tuning budget. The transferable lesson is the method, not
the ranking.
:::

## Readable, and small

```text
rec.autos            car, cars, engine, ford, oil, dealer, drive, price
sci.med              msg, doctor, disease, medical, pain, patients, treatment
sci.space            space, nasa, orbit, moon, launch, earth, spacecraft
talk.politics.guns   gun, guns, weapons, fbi, law, government, firearms
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="38%"}
::: {.stat}
[213×]{.bignum}

smaller as a sparse matrix: 2.8 MB instead of 601.6 MB
:::
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
- The terms with the largest coefficients for each class. [Dense representations rarely offer a term–coefficient mapping this clear]{.hl}
- 2,327 × 32,318, density 0.312% — 99.7% zeros
- No GPU needed: each of the six configurations finished in under 2 seconds on the laptop the measurements ran on. The 2.8 MB is the matrix alone; vocabulary, IDF and coefficients come on top
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
The other reason to care is that the model is *readable*. The table shows the
terms with the largest coefficients for each class of the TF-IDF plus logistic
regression model. The contribution to the score of a particular document depends
on the product of the coefficient and the feature value; a large coefficient is
not by itself a causal explanation. When you have to explain a model to a safety
board, a regulator or a sceptical plant manager, that readability makes it easier
to examine errors and discuss decisions. The trade-off against accuracy is set by
the requirements of the application.

The matrix stores 234,281 non-zeros. Dense float64 would need 601.6 MB; sparse
CSR needs 2.8 MB. End-to-end inference also includes preprocessing and
vectorization, and time depends on hardware and solver settings.

The chapter's strengths-and-limits table in brief. Strengths: a small sparse
matrix; readable; a strong baseline (0.853 here, and it beat averaged embeddings
in Chapter 3 and again on Turkish data in Chapter 4); no training data beyond
your own; with preprocessing, vocabulary, IDF and model fixed, the same input
gives the same output. Limits: no word order, no synonymy, no polysemy,
out-of-vocabulary terms can occur in new documents, and the scope of negation is
not encoded.

The two columns show the strengths and the limits of one and the same
representation; which side weighs more depends on what the task requires. When
exact term matching, speed and traceability matter, bag-of-words is a strong
starting option. When the task needs order or context, the representation has to
be extended: n-grams for local relations, character features for new forms, dense
and contextual representations for broader semantic relations.
:::

## Where this is actually deployed

- **Ticket triage at Uber (2018)** — COTA: TF-IDF and LSA; the cosine computed from LSA goes, with other features, into a random-forest ranker. Per the write-up, resolution time can fall by over 10%
- **Google's text classification guide** — TF-IDF n-grams are the most accurate of the encodings it compares; in its English experiments accuracy levels off around 20,000 features
- **Hybrid retrieval for RAG** — sparse BM25 catches the exact matches that embeddings can miss: part numbers, error codes, surnames (Ch. 20)
- **Spam and abuse filtering** — cheap enough to run on every message; feature hashing stores no explicit vocabulary, and in exchange different terms can share a column
- **Near-duplicate detection** — Google's work published in 2007 uses simhash fingerprints in web crawling; the other standard method is MinHash over shingles

::: {.src}
Uber Engineering 2018 · Google Developers 2022 · Weinberger et al. 2009 · Manku et al. 2007
:::

::: {.notes}
These examples show sparse text representations in use. Some rest on dated system
reports published by companies, others on method papers; read the architectures
as limited to the period those sources cover.

Uber's COTA: clean the text, tokenize, remove stop words, lemmatize, TF-IDF,
reduce with LSA. The cosine similarity goes, together with ticket and trip
features, into a random-forest matching model, and candidate solutions are ranked
by that model's score. The write-up compares this ranker with a multi-class
classifier fed the LSA topic vectors directly, on the same dataset and with the
same hyperparameters: 25% better in relative accuracy. That most LSA components
are close to zero is not the same kind of sparsity as the exact zeros of a count
matrix.

Google's guide: in its English experiments, features beyond about 20,000 selected
ones contribute very little and sometimes lower performance. That is not a fixed
threshold for every language. Our bigram result likewise shows that more features
bring no automatic gain; whether the two drops share a cause would have to be
tested.

Filtering: retraining time depends on data size, model and hardware. Feature
hashing maps terms to a fixed number of columns with a hash function, which makes
it harder to trace a coefficient back to a single term.

A shingle is a fixed-length window of words (or characters) slid across the
document; the windows overlap like roof tiles. The three-word shingles of *the
pump failed last night* are `the pump failed`, `pump failed last` and
`failed last night`. Shingles have the same structure as n-grams.

Search ranking is on the next slide.
:::

## BM25 — and why both its knobs are already familiar {.smaller}

$$\mathrm{BM25}(q, d) = \sum_{t \in q} \mathrm{idf}(t) \cdot \frac{c(t,d)\,(k_1 + 1)}{c(t,d) + k_1\!\left(1 - b + b\,\frac{|d|}{\mathrm{avgdl}}\right)}$$

- Lucene — so Elasticsearch and OpenSearch — scores documents with BM25 by default; BM25 comes from the TF-IDF family
- **$k_1$**: with document length fixed, the term-frequency contribution approaches the limit $k_1 + 1$. `sublinear_tf` slows down too, but $1 + \log(\text{tf})$ grows without bound
- **$b \in [0,1]$**: from ignoring length ($b = 0$) to dividing by length relative to the average ($b = 1$) — the concern L2 addresses, with a different formula
- Defaults of Lucene 9.12's `BM25Similarity`: $k_1 = 1.2$, $b = 0.75$

::: {.takeaway}
[For tasks it suits, such as text classification and lexical retrieval, build a TF-IDF baseline.]{.hl} If your transformer cannot beat it, you have learned something important about your data.
:::

::: {.src}
Robertson & Zaragoza 2009
:::

::: {.notes}
In this simplified formula the sum runs over the distinct terms of the query.
c(t,d) is the count of the term in the document, |d| the number of tokens in the
analysed document, and avgdl the average document length in the same collection.

Read the formula against what we just built. The idf factor is the same idea as
ours; BM25 uses a probabilistic variant. The fraction replaces raw term frequency
with a saturating one. And b handles the concern L2 normalization addresses —
long documents should not win on length alone — with a different formula. The two
are not the same operation.

BM25 is a common scoring method in many Lucene-based text search systems; it
cannot be assumed that every search box uses it. Elastic's "Practical BM25"
series explains the formula and its two tuning constants with detailed examples.

The chapter's practical rule: reach for TF-IDF when your labels are few, your
documents are long, your vocabulary is technical and exact match matters, or when
you need a baseline quickly.
:::

## Intuition check 1 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Your TF-IDF matrix has 200,000 columns and 5,000 rows. Should you worry?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Not about memory: storage scales with the number of *non-zeros*, not rows × columns
- The real worry is statistical — 200,000 features against 5,000 observations: [a p ≫ n problem]{.hl}, where regularization and the design of validation matter
- The usual answers: strong regularization (L2 or L1), and cutting the feature count with `min_df`
- On the four-category corpus, `min_df=5` takes 32,318 columns to 6,281 — 81% gone
- Not free: the deleted columns carry 11.6% of the token occurrences. `min_df=5` drops *every* term found in fewer than five documents
:::

::: {.notes}
The chapter's intuition checks: let students answer before revealing.

Why does `min_df` remove so many columns? The Zipf section showed it: most of the
vocabulary occurs in few documents, which can make the effect of those terms hard
to learn reliably. Some rare terms are nevertheless useful for telling particular
classes apart.

What goes is not only the terms seen once in total (hapax legomena); a term
repeated many times within a single document can go too. That is why the share of
columns removed and the share of token occurrences removed are reported
separately. Whether the trade is worth it is a question to measure; Exercise 4
asks for it.
:::

## Intuition check 2 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Should IDF be computed on the training set, or on all your data?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- In a supervised evaluation, **on the training portion only**, then applied unchanged to validation and test data. In cross-validation it is re-learned on every fold
- IDF is a parameter estimated from data: computing it over train + test leaks the test distribution into your features
- In `scikit-learn`: `fit_transform` on train, `transform` on test — calling `fit_transform` twice is a real and common bug
- In production the IDF vector is [a component you version and ship with the model]{.hl}, not something recomputed per batch
:::

::: {.notes}
Otherwise your features drift unnoticed as traffic changes. In search systems,
computing IDF from the indexed collection is a separate evaluation setting.

This answer comes back in the first interview question at the end of the
lecture.
:::

## Intuition check 3 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
A word appears in every document. What is its TF-IDF weight?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- `scikit-learn`'s smoothed formula: $\mathrm{df} = n$ gives $\ln\frac{1+n}{1+n} + 1 = 1$ — the IDF factor is 1, and the value before normalization is the term's TF
- The step that creates the gap to rarer terms is the multiplication by IDF; L2 divides the whole row by one norm
- The textbook unsmoothed $\log(n/\mathrm{df})$: exactly **0** — the term drops out of the vector
- `smooth_idf=False` still keeps the outer $+1$: $\ln(n/\mathrm{df}) + 1$. [It is 1 under that setting too; not the textbook formula]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Connect back to Step 4: `the` landed exactly on the floor of 1.0 in our
four-document corpus.
:::

## Intuition check 4 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Why do we normalize document vectors, but not feature columns?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- The two normalizations answer different questions. L2 row normalization brings document vectors to unit norm, so comparisons rest on the proportions of the weighted terms, not on size
- Subtracting non-zero column means and storing the result explicitly destroys sparsity: the 2.8 MB matrix needs about 601.6 MB dense
- Not every column scaling does: scaling without centring, such as `StandardScaler(with_mean=False)`, can keep the sparse structure
- [Sparsity is a constraint that determines which operations are practical]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
The numbers are the ones from the "Readable, and small" slide: the 2,327 ×
32,318 matrix of the classification experiment.
:::

## Intuition check 5 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Your search engine returns nothing for the part number “P-101”. Why?
:::

::: {.fragment}
```text
default    : ['101', '102', 'pump', 'tripped']
custom     : ['p-101', 'p-102', 'pump', 'tripped']
```

- Start by comparing the tokens the query analyser and the document analyser produce: the default `token_pattern=r"(?u)\b\w\w+\b"` needs two or more word characters and does not cross the hyphen
- `P-101` became `101` — the same token as a page number or a pressure reading. If both sides apply the same transformation, a match through `101` is still possible
- Nothing errors; accuracy just stays lower. [Print `get_feature_names_out()` and read it]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
`P-102` also became a bare number. The two are still different tokens, but the
equipment prefix is gone. Getting no result at all can also come from a mismatch
between the query and index analysers, or from other filters.

In technical domains tokenization errors of this kind lose important identifiers
and can seriously affect model performance. The habit that prevents it: after
fitting any vectorizer, print the feature names and read them. Exercise 2 is
exactly that.
:::

## Intuition check 6 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
When is a bag-of-words model the *right* choice in 2026?
:::

::: {.fragment}
When several of these hold together:

- very few labelled examples per class
- a domain-specific vocabulary where exact matching matters — part numbers, gene names, legal citations
- you must explain every prediction to someone with authority over you
- no GPU, or a hard latency budget
- long, topical documents rather than short, nuanced ones
:::

::: {.fragment}
And, in suitable classification and retrieval tasks, [as a baseline.]{.hl} With "our transformer gets 0.91" but no "TF-IDF gets 0.89", we do not know how much of a gain 0.91 is.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two clicks: the conditions, then its use as a baseline.

The last sentence points to Chapter 22 (Evaluating LLM Systems).
:::

## Interview question 1 of 2 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Your text classifier performs well offline and badly in production. Walk me through your debugging.
:::

::: {.fragment .compact}
A checklist, in cost order:

1. **Train/serve skew** — are the preprocessing rules, the vocabulary and the IDF values the same in both places, including the fitted `TfidfVectorizer`?
2. **Vocabulary drift** — new product names and error codes map to no column at all
3. **Distribution shift** in the label mix
4. **A leak in the offline evaluation** — e.g. fitting the vectorizer *before* the train/test split
5. Only then, the model
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.takeaway}
[The fitted vectorizer is a component stored with the model: save it, version it and ship it with the weights.]{.hl}
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Text representation is one of the core topics to study when preparing for applied
NLP interviews. The chapter has fourteen questions; these two are from the group
"testing whether you have shipped something".

On attribution, from the chapter: not every company attribution on pages headed
"NLP questions asked at Google and Amazon" rests on a verifiable source. The
chapter's question groups were prepared by drawing on the topics covered in two
free sources: Chip Huyen's *Introduction to Machine Learning Interviews* and the
*AIMLInterviews* repository. Neither attributes individual questions to a named
company.

"Serving" is the stage after training, where the model answers real requests.
Once fitted, the vectorizer is no longer just code; it carries two things learned
from the training data: the vocabulary and the IDF vector. Refitting it on
different data in production can change the column mapping or the weights, and
the problem then arises in the feature pipeline, before the classifier.
:::

## Interview question 2 of 2 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Design a system to detect near-duplicate documents in a corpus of 100 million.
:::

::: {.fragment .compact}
$\binom{10^8}{2} \approx 5 \times 10^{15}$ pairs — 58 days at a billion comparisons a second. [Never enumerate the pairs.]{.hl}

1. **Shingling** — each document becomes a set of 5–9-word windows; duplicates care about order
2. **Jaccard** $|A \cap B| / |A \cup B|$ — defines "near-duplicate"
3. **MinHash** — a 128-number signature; two signatures agree at a position with probability equal to the Jaccard similarity
4. **LSH** — splits signatures into bands and hashes them into buckets; only pairs that share a bucket become candidates. The number of bands sets the threshold
5. **Verify** — exact Jaccard on the candidate pairs only. Measure both the candidate cost and the recall
:::

::: {.src}
Broder 1997 · Indyk & Motwani 1998
:::

::: {.notes}
They are testing one reflex: do not try to look at every pair. The answer cannot
be "make it faster" — it has to be "never enumerate the pairs". Each step fixes
the problem the previous one leaves behind.

1. Why shingles rather than bag-of-words: two documents using the same words in a
   different order are not duplicates, yet bag-of-words gives them the same
   vector.
2. Jaccard is the right measure; the problem is computing it — the sets are large
   and there are still 5 × 10¹⁵ pairs.
3. MinHash: compare 128 numbers instead of intersecting large sets; storage drops
   to a few hundred bytes per document. The pair count is still 5 × 10¹⁵.
4. LSH: split the signature into b bands of r rows (b × r = 128), hash each band
      into a bucket, and call two documents candidates only if they share a bucket in
   at least one band. With a suitable data distribution and parameters this cuts the
   number of pairs to examine substantially; the number of candidates can still grow
   quadratically in large buckets, and LSH can miss some similar pairs.
5. A manageable number of pairs, not billions.

This chapter's material is the *first* step, and it matters more than it looks:
did you case-fold, strip punctuation, use character windows instead of word
windows — each changes what counts as a duplicate.
:::

## Exercises (1 of 2)

::: {.compact}
1. **Tokenizer economics.** Take a paragraph of your own technical writing in Turkish and its English translation, and count tokens under two tokenizers. First compute the ratio of token counts in the two languages; then estimate the annual cost at 100,000 requests per month with dated unit prices of a model you choose. Report input and output tokens separately.
2. **Break the vectorizer.** Fit a `CountVectorizer` on ten documents from your own domain and print `get_feature_names_out()`. Find at least two wrong tokens. If the problem is token boundaries fix it with `token_pattern`, otherwise with lowercasing or preprocessing; report what each change fixes and which new errors it could introduce.
3. **Derive it by hand.** Compute the TF-IDF vector for d3 with pen and paper, then verify against `TfidfVectorizer`. If they disagree, compare the TF definition, the IDF formula, the L2 normalization, the tokens, the column order and the rounding.
4. **Replicate and extend.** Reproduce the classification table, then add TF-IDF with `min_df=5`. Compare the two configurations on a validation portion split off from the training data, by accuracy, feature count, memory and time; use the test set only after the choice is made.
:::

::: {.notes}
The chapter's eight exercises, over two slides.

Exercise 3: with the same definitions and enough precision, the hand computation
and the library should agree within numerical tolerance.
:::

## Exercises (2 of 2)

::: {.compact}
5. **Find the negation failure.** Construct two documents from your own field with opposite operational meaning and TF-IDF cosine similarity above 0.9. Then write a design-review sentence explaining why a high cosine alone does not show that two documents express the same decision.
6. **Zipf on your own data.** Plot rank against frequency on log-log axes for a corpus you own. Does the line look straight? What are the top five tokens — is any of them an artifact like `'ax`?
7. **The interview exercise.** Work through the five-document TF-IDF ranking problem in §8.2.1 of Chip Huyen's book with pen and paper, including its follow-up on a document that mentions the query term three times. Before checking with the library, define the term set, the mappings between word forms (`birds → bird`) and the TF-IDF variant.
8. **Measure the Turkish token cost over many examples.** Collect 50–100 sentence pairs from a parallel text; for each tokenizer measure the Turkish/English token ratio per pair and the tokens per 1,000 code points in each language. Report the median and the interquartile range.
:::

::: {.notes}
In Exercise 7's follow-up, look at both the contribution of the repeated term to
the numerator and the change in the normalization denominator. With the other
variables fixed, BM25 brings the term-frequency contribution towards a finite
limit; `sublinear_tf` only slows its growth. Link:
https://huyenchip.com/ml-interviews-book/contents/8.2.1-natural-language-processing.html
:::

::: {.notes}
A selection from the chapter's list; the rest, for students who want more:

- Karpathy's video is two hours implementing BPE from scratch, including the
  Unicode handling the chapter measures on Turkish; minbpe is a few hundred lines
  of clean Python that build a GPT-grade tokenizer.
- 3Blue1Brown, *Large Language Models explained briefly*: seven minutes, a short
  visual introduction to how text is turned into a numerical representation.
- Jurafsky & Martin: the numbers belong to the online draft of August 19, 2026 and
  change between releases; PPMI is in Appendix J. When you use the numbers given
  in older sources, check the table of contents of the draft they refer to.
- Manning, Raghavan & Schütze: also the pages on stemming and lemmatization and on
  BM25. Free in full.
- Silge & Robinson, *Text Mining with R*: for statisticians who think in data
  frames rather than matrices, its TF-IDF chapter may click faster.
- Hugging Face course: the BPE lesson is the direct sequel to our toy
  implementation.
- tiktoken: the library used for the cost measurements.
- scikit-learn docs: read once properly and most "why don't my numbers match the
    book" questions disappear; its 20 Newsgroups classification example can be used
  to extend our experiment.
- Stanford CS276 (Information Retrieval and Web Search): the public course closest
  to this chapter's scope; CS224N picks up where Chapter 3 begins.
- Elena Voita's NLP Course For You: a lesson that explains the move from sparse
  counts to dense word vectors with visual examples.
:::
